https://www.bursa.ro/targu-mures-enters-.text: Târgu Mureş has been officially included in two European networks dedicated to the conservation and promotion of Art Nouveau heritage, the Reseau Art Nouveau Network and the Art Nouveau European Route. The accession, carried out by Visit Mureş, Târgu Mureş City Hall and the Mureş County Museum, aims to increase the international visibility of the city and the development of cultural tourism. *Over 150 buildings with Art Nouveau elements According to the Visit Mureş Association, the official representation of the municipality in the two European structures will be ensured directly by the tourism promotion organization. The accession places Târgu Mureş in an international network of cities that conserve, research and promote the Art Nouveau heritage and the Secession style, contributing to increasing the visibility of the municipality in the European cultural tourism circuit. "Târgu Mureş has one of the richest Art Nouveau architectural profiles in Romania,” claims Visit Mureş. According to the association, over 150 buildings in the urban area retain original elements of this style, from facades and architectural ornaments to ironwork, decorative details and stained glass. Among the representative buildings are the Palace of Culture and the Administrative Palace, two of the city's main architectural landmarks. *Heritage, transformed into a tourist resource Membership in the two European networks has not only a heritage conservation and research component, but also one related to tourism promotion. Visit Mureş believes that the inclusion of the municipality in these structures can strengthen Târgu Mureş's position in the European community interested in Secession heritage and can contribute to attracting new flows of tourists interested in architecture and culture. To mark the membership, the association launched a bilingual brochure dedicated to the local Secession heritage. The material presents the most important historical monument buildings and includes their technical descriptions. At the same time, the brochure proposes an urban itinerary for tourists, designed to facilitate the discovery of the main architectural landmarks of the municipality. *A new positioning for cultural tourism By being included in the Reseau Art Nouveau Network and the Art Nouveau European Route, Târgu Mureş can more effectively capitalize on its architectural heritage in a specialized European circuit. For the city, the stakes are both the preservation of historical buildings and their transformation into a cultural and tourist resource. The Art Nouveau heritage can thus become a distinctive element of the identity of the municipality and an additional argument for including Târgu Mureş in European cultural tourism itineraries. The partnership between the local administration, museum institutions and the tourism promotion organization provides, in this context, the framework for a coordinated promotion of the local architectural heritage outside Romania. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9p8.text: Image source, Corbis via Getty Image Image caption, The US has been sending migrants who cannot be deported to their home nations to other countries instead By Basillioh Rukanga Published 8 October 2026 Campaign group Human Rights Watch (HRW) says the deportation of migrants from the US to third-party African countries is against the law and exploits suffering to deter migration. "Many, if not most" of the deportees have no practical option but to return to their home countries regardless of the harm they face there, HRW says in a report. Since Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025, more than 500 people have been sent to African countries where they are not citizens, the group says, citing US data. The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said "third country removals are an essential public safety tool that remove the most dangerous criminal illegal aliens from our streets". Tackling immigration was one of Trump's key pledges during the 2024 election. Eswatini, which welcomed 32 deportees from the US, says three people - from Yemen, Belize and Laos - "voluntarily departed" to their home countries recently. According to HRW, some of the countries accepting the deportees have "arbitrarily detained" or sent them to their home countries, where they face "the risk of persecution or torture". The group said that people sent to Eswatini, Ghana and South Sudan, had been arbitrarily detained and faced ill-treatment while in detention. In Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea and Ghana, the deportees had been sent to their countries of origin despite the risk of "violating the principle of nonrefoulement [that people should not be sent to a country where they face torture, cruel treatment, or threats to their life and freedom]", it said. The group cited an unnamed US official as having told a Senate hearing that the point for the administration was that it could "threaten people that they will literally be dropped in the middle of nowhere". "The point is to scare people," HRW said. "Deporting people to countries where they have never set foot is part of a US policy designed to cause human suffering as a means to deter migration," said Michael Garcia Bochenek, the group's interim US programme director. In a statement from to the BBC, DHS said: "ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] is given diplomatic assurances from destination countries that the illegal aliens being removed there will be safe. When an individual is no longer in ICE custody, ICE is no longer responsible for them." White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told the BBC that those being sent to third countries were those whose home nations refused to take them or who had court orders preventing them being sent home. "Any illegal alien who wants to go home, we will arrange a free flight for them and give them a $3,000 check," she said. None of the African countries named has commented on the report. Deported from the US to Ghana then 'dumped' at the border: Nigerian man speaks out Published 3 October 2025 However, while announcing the recent departure of three migrants on Wednesday, Eswatini said that it was committed to ensuring that the "rights, dignity and well-being of third-country nationals were respected and protected". HRW said it interviewed 24 third-country nationals in six countries - Cameroon, Central African Republic, Democratic Republic of Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Eswatini and South Sudan. Some described to the group "abusive treatment" during their deportation flights, including being chained for about 18 hours and with no knowledge of their destination. They were also "denied access to essential medication, and often did not receive sufficient food or water". "The opaque deals that facilitate these transfers, some of which are still secret, are part of a US policy that violates international human rights law," HRW says. According to the report, at least a dozen people who identified as lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender (LGBT) were sent to African states that criminalise same-sex relations. Among them were refugees granted protection in the US based on the likelihood they would be persecuted back home because of their orientation or gender identity. In November, a Nigerian man deported from the US initially to Ghana expressed his fears to the BBC after he and five others were secretly transferred to Togo. He spoke of his fears about returning to Nigeria, where his association with a separatist activist group could lead to his arrest and torture. In DR Congo, HRW says it was told by a US lawyer that of the 15 people from Colombia, Peru and Ecuador deported to the country in April, none remained there by late September, with 11 having returned to their home countries. "The uncertainty and other conditions they faced in the Democratic Republic of Congo call into question whether these returns to countries of origin were voluntary," the group said. Equatorial Guinea, which received 65 people, quickly sent at least two people to their home countries, HRW said. Burundi announced late last month that it had agreed to take in migrants deported from the US. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6d9.text: Figure caption, How day of protests unfolded as disorder breaks out across France By Jack Burgess Published 17 October 2026 Violence broke out across France on Saturday during the latest day of demonstrations against hardship in schools and the cost of living. At least 1,200 people were arrested during what the French government described as an "escalation in violence" alongside an estimated 550,000 taking to the streets. In Paris, there were significant clashes into the evening with riot police, who used tear gas and water cannon on crowds. Buildings were set alight in the capital and other areas, including in Limoges where a large fire in the town hall caused the roof to partly collapse. Looting broke out in several cities, with widespread vandalism targeting city halls and businesses also reported. Figure caption, Watch: Moment historic French town hall spire collapses in flames amid protests Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu said 150 police officers were injured in the unrest. In Paris, the main march appeared to be largely peaceful during the afternoon. A group of young people told the BBC they were "pacifists" who are "just trying to make things change, but nothing is moving". However, as the day wore on some groups lit fires in the street and torched vehicles, including in iconic locations in the city centre like the Place de la RÃ©publique. Shops were ransacked, at least one restaurant was gutted by fire, and the BBC saw fighting breaking out among some of the groups. Riot police were seen charging at one crowd in central Paris and hitting several people with batons. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, La Barrique bar in Paris was set on fire In Lyon, Mayor GrÃ©gory Doucet said the burning of the city's tourist office was "a tragedy" for the city, telling BFMTV "it breaks our hearts because it's a very iconic, well-known historic building". Local police said "hostile individuals" prevented firefighters from safely tackling the blaze. Fire crews also battled the fire at Limoges town hall, which the local prefecture said caused part of the building to collapse. A young man "had his hand blown off by a grenade" in Saint-Ãtienne, the south-eastern city's Mayor RÃ©gis Juanico said on social media, adding: "Such a tragedy should never have happened." The interior ministry said the protests involved "targeted acts of violence" from "hooded individuals" in places, including parts of the capital and also Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse and Angers. Damage to buildings was reported across France, including in Grenoble, Avignon, Pau, Montpellier and Valence. Clothes and food shops were raided in Paris, while an Apple store in Lille was broken into and emptied. Footage authenticated by BBC Verify showed a tourist train in Grenoble being driven by masked men along a narrow street in the city centre towards at least three riot police officers. Image source, Reuters Image caption, A car was set alight at the Place de la RÃ©publique in Paris Hundreds of thousands of students have protested in recent weeks over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycÃ©es - secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds. On Saturday, their numbers were bolstered by trade union members and other protest groups. These groups include the so-called gilets jaunes 'yellow vest' movement, who demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for over a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history. While France is no stranger to outbreaks of protest and disorder, this round comes as the country heads into a period of deep political uncertainty. French President Emmanuel Macron will leave office next year and polls suggest April's presidential election could come down to a fight between the leader of the National Rally, Marine Le Pen, and Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon of the hard-left La France Insoumise party. The latter took part in demonstrations in France and later accused police officers of "unleashing" on protesters, while condemning looting and arson. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Rapid-response riot police were deployed in Paris Prime Minister Lecornu said his comments were "dangerous and cynical". He earlier said police had faced "violence of extreme intensity" and some groups were using the protests as a "warm-up" for the presidential elections, adding: "No-one will impose their political agenda through violence." Le Pen said "legitimate demands" voiced by protesters had been "held hostage by the far left", accusing MÃ©lenchon of fuelling the violence. French President Emmanuel Macron said: "Those who have broken, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished." The government has made apparent attempts at concessions, with Education Minister Ãdouard Geffray promising 3,000 extra supply teachers, during a television interview on 8 October. However, the protests have continued and intensified.
